## Choose **one** prompt to answer

> 

> **Prompt B:** `r params$p2`

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Response

If I were analyzing a survey dataset and noticed that some answers were missing or looked really weird, I know there are a few things I could do, like deleting those responses, filling in values, or recoding things so they look more organized. But the choice I make shouldn’t just be random. It should depend on why the data looks that way and what would keep the research as honest and fair as possible. The first thing I’d think about is why the data is missing. Sometimes people skip a question by accident, which is harmless. But other times, the missing responses might come from something more meaningful. For example, maybe certain types of people avoid answering a sensitive question, or maybe the question was confusing and everyone misunderstood it. If the missing answers seem random and only affect a tiny part of the dataset, deleting them might be okay. But if a lot of people skipped the same question, or if removing them would shrink the sample too much, deleting data could totally mess up the results. Another option is "imputation," which basically means guessing what the missing answer could have been using other information from the survey. This keeps the dataset bigger, but it also comes with risks because the imputed values aren’t real answers. They could change the results without you realizing it. If the problem is messy formatting or inconsistent categories, then recoding or organizing the data is fine as long as I’m not changing the meaning of anyone’s response. Overall, what should guide my choices is transparency and fairness. I should explain exactly what I changed and why. Good data cleaning isn’t about making results look perfect, but it’s about keeping the research honest and trustworthy.

## Word Count & Range Check

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
get_response_text <- function() {
  f <- knitr::current_input()
  if (is.null(f) || !file.exists(f)) return("")
  x <- readLines(f, warn = FALSE)
  # Find the lines that EXACTLY match the start/end markers
  s <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-START -->$", x)
  e <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-END -->$", x)
  if (length(s) != 1 || length(e) != 1 || e <= s) return("")
  paste(x[(s + 1L):(e - 1L)], collapse = "\n")
}
count_words <- function(txt) {
  # Remove code blocks and inline code before counting
  txt <- gsub("```[\\s\\S]*?```", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  txt <- gsub("`[^`]*`", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Keep letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens, and apostrophes
  txt <- gsub("[^\\p{L}\\p{N}\\s'-]", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Split by whitespace and count non-empty words
  words <- unlist(strsplit(txt, "\\s+", perl = TRUE))
  words <- words[nzchar(words)]
  length(words)
}
txt <- get_response_text()
n <- count_words(txt)
minw <- as.integer(params$word_min)
maxw <- as.integer(params$word_max)
in_range <- n >= minw && n <= maxw
cat(sprintf("**Word count:** %d  \n", n))
cat(sprintf("**Required range (%s):** %d–%d words  \n",
            toupper(params$course), minw, maxw))
cat(if (in_range) "**Status:** ✅ In range\n" else "**Status:** ❌ Out of range\n")
```
